In [[mathematics]], specifically [[Group theory#Finite group theory|finite group theory]], the '''uniqueness case''' is one of the three possibilities for [[group (mathematics)|group]]s of [[characteristic 2 type]] given by the [[trichotomy theorem]].

The uniqueness case covers groups ''G'' of characteristic&nbsp;2 type with ''e''(''G'')&nbsp;≥&nbsp;3 that have an almost strongly {{nowrap|''p''-embedded}} maximal {{nowrap|2-local}} subgroup for all [[prime number|primes]] ''p'' whose {{nowrap|2-local}} {{nowrap|''p''-rank}} is sufficiently large (usually at least&nbsp;3).
{{harvs|txt|last=Aschbacher|year1=1983a|year2=1983b}} [[mathematical proof|proved]] that there are no [[finite simple group]]s in the uniqueness case.
